title: Book 8
paragraphs: My God, let me remember with thanksgiving, and confess to you, your mercies toward me. Let my bones be soaked in your love, and let them say to you, "Who is like you, Lord?" You have broken my chains apart; I will offer you the sacrifice of thanksgiving. And I will tell how you broke them, so that all who worship you, when they hear this, will say, "Blessed be the Lord, in heaven and on earth, great and wonderful is his name." Your words had lodged fast in my heart, and I was hedged in on every side by you. Of your eternal life I was now certain, though I saw it only dimly, as through a clouded glass. Yet I had stopped doubting that there was an incorruptible reality, the source of all other reality; and I no longer wanted to be more certain of you, but more steady in you. But as for my life here in time, everything was still unsettled, and my heart had to be purged of the old leaven. The Way, the Savior himself, pleased me well, but I still shrank from walking its narrow path. And you put it into my mind, and it seemed good to me, to go to Simplicianus, who seemed to me a good servant of yours; your grace shone in him. I had also heard that from his very youth he had lived most devoted to you. Now he was advanced in years, and given so great an age spent following your ways with such zeal, he seemed to me likely to have gained much experience — and so he had. Out of that store I wanted him to tell me, once I had laid my anxieties before him, which was the best way for someone in my condition to walk in your paths.

For I saw the church full, and one person went this way and another that; but I was unhappy that I was leading a worldly life — indeed, now that ambition and the hope of profit no longer inflamed my desires as they once had, it was a very heavy burden to bear so heavy a bondage. Compared with your sweetness and the beauty of your house, which I loved, those things no longer delighted me. But I was still enslaved by the love of a woman; and the Apostle did not forbid me to marry, though he urged something better, above all wishing that everyone were as he was. But being weak, I chose the easier path, and this alone was enough to toss me back and forth in everything else, worn out and wasted by withering anxieties, because in other matters I was forced against my will to shape myself to a married life, to which I was given over and enslaved. I had heard from the mouth of the Truth that there were eunuchs who had made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven — but, he said, let the one who can accept this, accept it. Surely everyone is foolish who does not know God, and cannot find him who is good out of the good things that can be seen. But I was no longer caught in that foolishness; I had risen above it, and by the shared testimony of all your creatures I had found you our Creator, and your Word, God together with you, and with you one God, through whom you created all things. There is yet another kind of the ungodly, who, knowing God, did not glorify him as God, nor give him thanks. Into this too I had fallen, but your right hand upheld me and took me out of it, and set me down where I could recover. For you have said to man, "Look, the fear of the Lord is wisdom," and, "Do not wish to seem wise," because those who claimed to be wise became fools. But I had now found the goodly pearl, which I ought to have bought by selling everything I had — and I hesitated.

So I went to Simplicianus, the man through whose hand Ambrose (now a bishop) had received your grace, and whom Ambrose truly loved as a father. I told him about the twists and turns of my wanderings. But when I mentioned that I had read certain books of the Platonists, which Victorinus, once a professor of rhetoric at Rome (who I had heard died a Christian), had translated into Latin, he expressed his joy that I had not stumbled instead onto the writings of other philosophers, full of falsehoods and deceptions built on the elementary principles of this world, whereas the Platonists in many ways lead toward belief in God and his Word. Then, to encourage me toward the humility of Christ, hidden from the wise and revealed to little children, he told me about Victorinus himself, whom he had known very closely while at Rome — and he told me something I will not keep back. It contains great praise of your grace, and deserves to be confessed to you: how that elderly man, so learned and so skilled in the liberal arts, who had read and weighed so many works of the philosophers, the teacher of so many distinguished senators, who — as a mark of his outstanding public service, something the world regards as a high honor — had both earned and received a statue in the Roman Forum; this man, who to that late age worshiped idols and took part in the sacrilegious rites to which almost all the Roman nobility were given over, and who had filled the people with love of
Anubis, barking god, and all The monster gods of every kind, who fought against Neptune, Venus, and Minerva;

gods whom Rome had once conquered and now worshiped, all of which the elderly Victorinus had for so many years defended with thundering eloquence — this man no longer felt shame at becoming a child of your Christ, and the newborn infant of your font, bending his neck to the yoke of humility and bowing his proud forehead beneath the disgrace of the cross.

Lord, Lord, who bowed the heavens and came down, who touched the mountains and they smoked — by what means did you find your way into that man's chest? He used to read the holy Scripture, Simplicianus told me, and searched most eagerly into all the Christian writings, and would say to Simplicianus — not openly, but privately, as one friend to another — "Understand that I am already a Christian." Simplicianus would answer, "I will not believe it, and I will not count you among Christians, unless I see you in the church of Christ." Victorinus would reply, mocking, "Is it walls, then, that make Christians?" And he said many times that he was already a Christian, and Simplicianus gave the same answer just as many times, and the joke about the "walls" was raised again just as often by Victorinus. He was afraid of offending his friends, proud worshipers of demons, and thought that from the height of their Babylonian rank — like cedars of Lebanon, which the Lord had not yet brought down — the full weight of their hostility would fall on him. But once, through reading and steady reflection, he had grown firm, and began to fear that Christ would deny him before the holy angels if he himself was now afraid to acknowledge Christ before men; and it struck him that he was guilty of a serious wrong, being ashamed of the sacraments of the humility of your Word while feeling no shame at all for the sacrilegious rites of those proud demons, whose pride he had imitated and whose rites he had taken up. So he grew bold in the face of that emptiness and ashamed instead in the face of truth, and suddenly and unexpectedly he said to Simplicianus, as Simplicianus himself told me, "Let us go to the church; I want to become a Christian." Simplicianus, unable to contain his joy, went with him. And once Victorinus had been admitted to the first sacrament and become a catechumen, it was not long before he further gave in his name so that he might be reborn through baptism, to the astonishment of Rome and the rejoicing of the church. The proud saw it and were furious; they ground their teeth and wasted away. But the Lord God was the hope of your servant, and he paid no attention to vanities and lying madness.

Then, when the hour came for him to make his profession of faith — which at Rome those approaching your grace deliver from a raised platform, in the sight of the whole body of the faithful, in a set form of words committed to memory — the priests, he said, offered Victorinus the option, as was customary for those thought likely to be frightened by their own shyness, of making his profession more privately. But he chose instead to declare his salvation in the presence of the whole holy assembly. "For it was not salvation that he had taught in his rhetoric classes, and yet he had professed that publicly enough — so how much less should he, in pronouncing your word, be afraid of your gentle flock, when in delivering his own words he had never feared a raving crowd!" So then, when he went up to make his profession, everyone who knew him whispered his name to one another with a voice of delight. And who there did not know him? A low murmur ran through the mouths of the whole rejoicing crowd: "Victorinus! Victorinus!" There was a sudden burst of joy at the sight of him; just as suddenly they fell silent so they could hear him. He spoke the true faith with splendid boldness, and everyone wanted to draw him into their very heart — and by their love and joy, that is exactly what they did; such were the hands with which they drew him in.

Good God, what happens in a person, that he rejoices more over the rescue of a soul given up for lost, and saved from a greater danger, than he would if there had always been hope for that soul, or the danger had been smaller? So you too, merciful Father, rejoice more over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance. And we too listen with great joy, whenever we hear how the sheep that had strayed is carried home on the shepherd's shoulders, to the joy of all the angels; and how the lost coin is returned to your treasury, with the neighbors rejoicing alongside the woman who found it; and the joy of the solemn service in your house moves us to tears when we hear read there the story of your younger son, that he was dead and has come back to life, was lost and is found. For you rejoice in us, and in your holy angels, holy through holy love. For you are always the same, and everything that does not remain the same, or last forever, you nevertheless always know in the same unchanging way.

What, then, happens in the soul, that it takes more delight in finding or getting back the things it loves than it would if it had always had them? And other things bear witness to this too; everything is full of witnesses crying out, "So it is." The victorious general celebrates his triumph, yet he would not have won had he not first fought, and the greater the danger in the battle, the greater the joy in the triumph. The storm tosses the sailors and threatens shipwreck; everyone turns pale at the approach of death; then sky and sea grow calm, and they are overjoyed, precisely because they had been so afraid. A friend is sick, and his pulse warns of danger; everyone who longs for his recovery is sick at heart along with him. He is restored, though he does not yet walk with his former strength, and yet there is such joy as there was not when before he walked sound and strong. Indeed, people gain the very pleasures of human life through difficulties — not only the difficulties that fall on us unlooked-for and against our will, but even trouble that we choose for ourselves and go looking for. Eating and drinking give no pleasure unless hunger and thirst have first gnawed at us. Men given to drink eat certain salty foods on purpose, to work up an uncomfortable thirst, which the drink then relieves, producing pleasure. It is also the custom that an engaged woman should not be handed over to her husband right away, in case, once married, he should think cheaply of her, whom as his betrothed he had longed for.

This law holds in shameful and cursed pleasure; it holds in permitted and lawful pleasure; it holds in the very purest and highest form of friendship; it holds in the one who was dead and has come back to life, who had been lost and was found. Everywhere the greater joy is ushered in by the greater pain. What does this mean, Lord my God, when you yourself are everlasting joy to yourself, and some things around you rejoice in you without end? What does this mean, that this portion of things ebbs and flows in this way, alternately displeased and then reconciled? Is this the measure allotted to them? Is this all you have assigned to them — when from the highest heavens to the lowest earth, from the beginning of the world to the end of the ages, from the angel down to the worm, from the very first motion to the very last, you set each thing in its place and bring each to completion in its own season, everything good after its kind? How wretched I am! How high are you in the highest, and how deep in the deepest! And you never leave us, and yet we so rarely return to you.

Rise up, Lord, and act; stir us up and call us back; kindle us and draw us on; set us on fire, grow sweet to us — let us now love, let us run. Do not many return to you out of a deeper pit of blindness than Victorinus's, and draw near, and are given light, receiving that Light which gives to those who receive it the power to become your children? But if they are less well known to the world, then even those who do know them rejoice less for them. For when many people rejoice together, each of them has a fuller joy, because they catch fire from one another. Again, those who are known to many influence more people toward salvation, and lead the way for many to follow. And so those who went before them also rejoice greatly over them, because their joy is not for themselves alone. Far be it that in your dwelling place the rich should be honored above the poor, or the noble above the common — since you have instead chosen the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and the lowly things of this world, and the despised things, and the things that are nothing, so that you might reduce to nothing the things that are. And yet even that least of your apostles, through whose tongue you spoke these very words, once he had conquered the pride of Paulus the proconsul, in his war of faith, and brought him under the easy yoke of your Christ, to become a citizen of the great King — he too was pleased, in testimony to so great a victory, to be called Paul instead of his former name, Saul. For the enemy is more thoroughly beaten in someone he has a firmer hold on, and through whom he has a hold on more people. And he holds the proud more firmly, because of their high rank, and through them he holds many more, because of their authority. So the more welcome it was that the heart of Victorinus — which the devil had held as an impregnable stronghold — and the tongue of Victorinus — that mighty and sharp weapon with which he had struck down so many — should be taken; all the more should your children rejoice all the more abundantly, because our King bound the strong man, and they saw his weapons taken from him, cleaned, and made fit for your honor, made useful to the Lord for every good work.

But when that man of yours, Simplicianus, told me this story about Victorinus, I burned to imitate him — which was exactly why he had told it to me. And when he added how, in the days of the Emperor Julian, a law was passed forbidding Christians to teach the liberal arts or oratory, and how Victorinus, obeying that law, chose to give up his school of words rather than give up your Word, by which you make eloquent the tongues of the mute — he struck me as not so much courageous as fortunate, for having found in this way the chance to devote himself to you alone. That was exactly what I was longing for, bound as I was, not by another's chains, but by my own iron will. My will was in the enemy's grip, and out of it he had forged a chain and bound me fast. For out of a perverse will, desire had been made; and desire indulged became habit; and habit not resisted became necessity. By these links, joined one to another — which is why I called it a chain — a hard slavery held me captive. But the new will, which had begun to stir in me, to serve you freely and to long to enjoy you, God, the only certain sweetness, was not yet strong enough to overcome the old will, hardened by long years. So my two wills, one old and one new, one carnal and the other spiritual, fought within me, and by their conflict tore my soul apart.

So I understood, from my own experience, what I had read — that the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. I was truly on both sides, yet more myself in the will I approved of in myself than in the one I disapproved of. For in the latter, it was for the most part no longer really myself, because in much of it I was enduring something against my will rather than acting willingly. And yet it was through me that habit had gained this power to war against me, because I had come, of my own will, to a place I did not want to be. And who has any right to object, if the sinner suffers a just punishment? I no longer even had my old excuse — that I still hesitated to rise above the world and serve you because the truth was not yet fully certain to me — for now it was certain. But still bound in service to the earth, I refused to fight under your banner, and I feared being freed of all my burdens just as much as we ought to fear being burdened with them. So I was pleasantly weighed down by the baggage of this present world, as if asleep, and the thoughts in which I meditated on you were like the efforts of someone trying to wake, who is nonetheless overcome by heavy drowsiness and sinks back into it. And just as no one wants to sleep forever, and everyone in their right mind agrees that being awake is better, yet a person, feeling a heavy sluggishness through all his limbs, still often puts off shaking off sleep, and — half annoyed with himself — nevertheless gives in to it with pleasure even after it is time to get up, so I was certain that it would be far better for me to surrender myself to your love than to give myself over to my own desire; but while the first path satisfied me and had won the argument, the second still pleased me and held me captive. I had nothing to answer you when you called to me, "Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will give you light." And though you showed me on every side that what you said was true, I, convicted by the truth, had absolutely nothing to answer, except only those dull, drowsy words: "In a moment." "In a little while." "Just leave me a little longer." But "in a moment, in a moment" never had a moment, and my "little while" stretched on and on; it was no use that I delighted in your law according to my inner self, when another law in my body's members rose up in rebellion against the law of my mind, and dragged me captive under the law of sin at work in my members. For the law of sin is the sheer force of habit, by which the mind is dragged along and held fast even against its will — but justly so, since it fell into that habit of its own free will. Who, then, would rescue me, wretch that I was, from this body of death, except your grace alone, through Jesus Christ our Lord?

And now I will tell how you freed me from the bonds of desire, by which I was bound most tightly to the lust of the flesh, and from the drudgery of worldly business, and confess it to your name, Lord, my helper and my redeemer. Amid mounting anxiety, I went on with my usual work, sighing to you every day. I went to your church whenever I was free from the business under whose weight I groaned. Alypius was with me, now released from his legal practice after his third term of service, and waiting for buyers for his legal advice — just as I sold the skill of speaking, if indeed that skill can even be taught. Nebridius, out of consideration for our friendship, had agreed to teach under Verecundus, a citizen and grammar teacher of Milan, and a very close friend to all of us, who had urgently asked, and by the claim of friendship demanded from our circle, the kind of loyal help he badly needed. Nebridius was not drawn to this by any desire for advantage — he could have made far more of his learning had he wanted to — but as a most kind and generous friend, he would not refuse a good office or make light of our request. But he handled it very carefully, avoiding becoming known to powerful people of this world, avoiding the distraction that would bring, and wanting to keep as many hours as possible free and unhurried, to seek, read, or hear something about wisdom.

One day, then, with Nebridius away (I don't recall why), a man named Ponticianus came to visit Alypius and me — a countryman of ours, being African, and holding high office at the imperial court. What he wanted with us I don't know, but we sat down to talk, and it happened that he noticed a book lying on a gaming table in front of us; he picked it up, opened it, and, to his surprise, found it was the Apostle Paul — for he had expected it to be one of the books I wore myself out teaching. At this he smiled, looked at me, and said how glad and surprised he was to find, on the spur of the moment, this book and no other lying open before my eyes. For he was a Christian, and baptized, and often bowed down before you our God in the church, in frequent and lengthy prayers. When I told him that I devoted a great deal of effort to those Scriptures, a conversation began, prompted by his account, about Antony the Egyptian monk — whose name stood in high repute among your servants, though up to that hour it was unknown to us. When he discovered this, he lingered on the subject even longer, telling us more and marveling at our ignorance of someone so remarkable. We stood there amazed, hearing of your wonderful works, so fully attested, in times so recent, almost our own, accomplished in the true faith and the Catholic Church. We were all amazed — we, that these things were so great, and he, that they had never reached us.

From there his talk turned to the communities in the monasteries, and their holy way of life, a sweet fragrance rising to you, and the fruitful deserts of the wilderness, of which we knew nothing. And there was a monastery at Milan, full of good brothers, just outside the city walls, under the fostering care of Ambrose — and we did not even know it. He went on talking, and we listened in tense silence. He told us then how one afternoon at Trier, while the Emperor was occupied with the games in the circus, he and three companions went out to walk in gardens near the city walls, and there, as they happened to walk in pairs, one walked apart with him, and the other two wandered off on their own; and these two, in their wandering, came upon a small cottage where some of your servants lived, poor in spirit, the kind to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs, and there they found a little book containing the life of Antony. One of them began to read it, and was struck with wonder, and caught fire as he read, and began, even as he read, to think about taking up such a life himself, and giving up his career in the world to serve you. And these two men were among those they call agents for public affairs. Then suddenly, filled with a holy love and a sober shame, angry with himself, he turned his eyes on his friend and said, "Tell me, please — what do we hope to gain from all this labor of ours? What are we aiming at? What are we working for? Can our ambitions at court rise any higher than to become friends of the Emperor? And even there, what is not fragile, and full of danger? And through how many dangers do we arrive only at a greater danger still? And when would we even get there? But a friend of God — if I want to be one, I can become one right now." So he spoke. And in the pain of labor toward a new life, he turned his eyes back to the book, and read on, and was changed within, where you could see it, and his mind was stripped bare of the world, as soon became clear. For as he read, and the waves of his heart rose and fell, he raged at himself for a while, then saw clearly, and resolved on the better course; and now belonging to you, he said to his friend, "Now I have broken free of those hopes of ours, and I am resolved to serve God, and I am starting on it, from this hour, in this place. If you don't want to follow my example, don't stand in my way." His friend answered that he would stay with him, to share in so glorious a reward, so glorious a service. So both of them, now yours, were building the tower, at the necessary cost of giving up everything they owned, and following you. Then Ponticianus and the other man who had been walking in a different part of the garden came looking for them in that same spot, and having found them, reminded them it was time to go back, since the day was far gone. But the two told them what they had resolved and decided, and how that will had begun and taken firm root in them, and begged the others, if they would not join them, at least not to hinder them. The other two, though nothing had changed in themselves, still wept for themselves (so he said), and warmly congratulated their friends, asking to be remembered in their prayers, and so, with their hearts still dragging on the earth, went off to the palace. But the other two, fixing their hearts on heaven, stayed on in the cottage. And both of them had brides waiting for them, who, when they heard of it, likewise dedicated their virginity to God.

Such was Ponticianus's story. But you, Lord, while he was speaking, turned me around to face myself, pulling me out from behind my own back, where I had placed myself to avoid looking at myself, and setting me squarely in front of my own face, so that I might see how foul I was, how crooked and stained, spotted and diseased. I saw it, and stood horrified; and there was nowhere I could find to run from myself. And whenever I tried to turn my eyes away from myself, he went on with his story, and you set me over against myself once more, and thrust me before my own eyes, so that I would find out my own wrongdoing and hate it. I had known it all along, but had pretended not to see it, shut my eyes to it, and forgotten it.

But now, the more passionately I loved those men whose healthy resolve I had just heard of — that they had given themselves wholly over to you to be healed — the more I loathed myself by comparison with them. For many years of mine — some twelve — had run out since my nineteenth, when, on reading Cicero's Hortensius, I had been stirred to an earnest love of wisdom; and still I kept putting off rejecting mere earthly happiness to devote myself to searching for that wisdom whose very search — not even the finding of it — was worth more than the treasures and kingdoms of the world, even if already found, and more than the pleasures of the body, even spread out around me for the taking. But wretched, most wretched creature that I was, in the very first days of my youth I had begged you for chastity, and said, "Give me chastity and self-control, only not yet." For I was afraid you would hear me too soon, and cure me too soon of the disease of lust, which I wanted satisfied rather than put out. And I had wandered through crooked paths in a sacrilegious superstition — not because I was truly convinced of it, but because I preferred it to the other beliefs, which I did not seek out in a religious spirit, but attacked with hostility.

And I had believed that the reason I kept putting off, day after day, rejecting the hopes of this world and following you alone was that nothing certain had yet appeared, to show me which way to go. But now the day had come when I was to be laid bare to myself, and my own conscience was to accuse me. "Where are you now, my tongue? You used to say that you didn't want to throw off the baggage of vanity for the sake of an uncertain truth — well, now it is certain, and that burden still weighs you down, while people who have not worn themselves out searching for it, who have not spent ten years or more thinking about it, have had their shoulders lightened and grown wings to fly away." So I was gnawed at within, and utterly overwhelmed with a horrible shame, while Ponticianus was saying all this. And once he had finished his story and the business that had brought him, he went on his way, and I turned back into myself. What did I not say against myself? With what lashes of condemnation did I not whip my soul, to make it follow me as I struggled to go after you! Yet it pulled back; it refused, but had no excuse to offer. All its arguments were used up and disproved; there remained only a mute shrinking back, and it feared, as it would fear death, to be held back from the flow of that habit by which it was wasting away to death.

Then, in this great inner struggle, which I had violently stirred up against my own soul, in the inner room of my heart, disturbed in mind and in face, I turned on Alypius. "What is wrong with us?" I cried out. "What is this? What did you just hear? The unlearned rise up and seize heaven by force — and we, with all our learning, but no heart, look at us, wallowing in flesh and blood! Are we ashamed to follow, because others have already gone ahead — and not ashamed that we are not even following at all?" Something like these words I spoke, and my fever of mind tore me away from him, while he, staring at me in astonishment, said nothing. For it was not my usual tone of voice, and my forehead, cheeks, eyes, complexion, and the very pitch of my voice expressed my mind more than the words I actually spoke. There was a small garden attached to our lodging, which we had the use of, as of the whole house, since our host, the master of the house, did not live there. The turmoil in my chest had driven me there, where no one could interfere with the fierce struggle I had entered into with myself, until it should come out however you knew it would — I did not know. I was only usefully torn apart, and dying in order to live, knowing what an evil thing I still was, and not knowing what good thing I was about to become. I withdrew, then, into the garden, and Alypius followed on my steps. For his being there did not lessen my privacy — how could he have left me alone, so disturbed? We sat down as far from the house as we could. I was troubled in spirit, most fiercely indignant that I was not entering into your will and covenant, my God, which all my bones cried out to me to enter, and praised to the skies. And to enter it we did not need ships, or chariots, or even our own feet — we did not need to go even as far as I had come from the house to the place where we were sitting. For to go there — no, even more, to actually arrive there — was nothing else but to will to go, but to will it resolutely and completely, not to twist and turn, this way and that, with a crippled, half-divided will, wrestling with itself, one part rising as the other sank.

At last, in the very fever of my indecision, I made with my body many of the motions that people sometimes want to make but cannot, if either they lack the limbs for it, or their limbs are bound, weakened by illness, or hindered in some other way. So if I tore my hair, struck my forehead, if I locked my fingers together and clasped my knee — I willed it, and I did it. But I could have willed it and not done it, if my limbs had not obeyed the power of motion. So many things, then, I did, in cases where "to will" was not the same as "to be able"; and yet I did not do the thing I longed to do incomparably more, and which soon after, once I willed it, I would be able to do — because soon after, once I willed it, I would will it completely. For in these bodily things, the ability and the will were one and the same, and to will was to do; and yet in this other matter it was not done — even though my body obeyed the weakest wish of my soul more readily, moving its limbs at the least nod, than my soul obeyed itself in carrying out, by will alone, this one great thing it willed.

Where does this monstrous condition come from? And to what end? Let your mercy shine so that I may ask — in case the hidden punishments imposed on human beings, and those darkest sufferings of the sons of Adam, can perhaps give me an answer. Where does this monstrous condition come from? And to what end? The mind commands the body, and it obeys at once; the mind commands itself, and is resisted. The mind commands the hand to move, and there is such readiness that the command can hardly be told apart from the obedience. Yet the mind is mind, and the hand is body. The mind commands the mind — itself — to will something, and yet it does not do it. Where does this monstrous condition come from? And to what end? It commands itself, I say, to will, and it would not give the command unless it already willed it, and yet what it commands does not happen. But it does not will entirely; therefore it does not command entirely. For it commands only to the extent that it wills, and the thing commanded fails to happen only to the extent that it does not will it. For it is the will that commands there be a will — not some other will, but itself. But it does not command entirely, and so what it commands does not fully exist. For if the will were whole and entire, it would not even need to command itself to exist, because it would already exist. So it is not some monstrous split, to will one thing in part and refuse it in part — it is a disease of the mind, that it does not rise up wholly, borne up by truth, weighed down by habit. And so there are two wills, because neither one is whole and entire — and what the one lacks, the other has.

Let them perish from your presence, God, as talkers of nonsense and seducers of the soul perish, who, noticing that in deliberating there are two wills, claim that we have two minds of two different kinds within us, one good and the other evil. They themselves are truly evil, as long as they hold these evil opinions; and they themselves will become good once they hold the truth and agree with the truth, so that your Apostle may say to them, "You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." But because they want to be light in themselves, not in the Lord, imagining the nature of the soul to be what God alone is, they turn into an even thicker darkness through a terrifying arrogance — because in this way they have gone even further from you, the true Light that enlightens everyone who comes into the world. Watch what you say, and be ashamed: come close to him and be given light, and your faces will not be put to shame. As for me, when I was deliberating about serving the Lord my God now, as I had long intended, it was I who was willing, I who was unwilling — I, I myself. I neither willed it entirely nor refused it entirely. So I was at war with myself, and torn apart by myself. And this tearing happened to me against my will, and yet it showed, not the presence of some other mind, but the punishment of my own. And so it was no longer I who was doing it, but the sin living in me — the punishment of a sin committed more freely, since I was a son of Adam.

For if there were as many contrary natures as there are conflicting wills, there would now be not just two, but many. If someone is deciding whether to go to the Manichees' meeting-house or to the theater, these Manichees cry out, "Look, here are two natures — one good, pulling this way, another bad, pulling back the other way. For where else could this hesitation between conflicting wills come from?" But I say that both are bad — the one that draws toward them just as much as the one that draws back toward the theater. But they refuse to believe that the will drawing toward them could be anything but good. What, then, if one of us were deciding, and, caught in the struggle of two wills, were torn between whether to go to the theater or to our church? Would these Manichees not also be caught, unsure what to answer? For either they must admit, however unwillingly, that the will drawing someone toward our church is just as good as the will of those who are caught up in the mysteries of their own sect; or they must suppose two evil natures and two evil souls fighting within one person, and then it would not be true, as they claim, that one is good and the other bad; or else they must be converted to the truth, and stop denying that when someone deliberates, it is one single soul wavering between conflicting wills.

Let them no longer say, then, when they notice two conflicting wills in one person, that the conflict is between two opposing souls, of two opposing substances, from two opposing sources, one good and the other bad. For you, true God, disprove them, check them, and convict them — as, for instance, when both wills are bad, and someone deliberates whether he should kill a man by poison or by the sword; whether he should seize this piece of someone else's property or that one, since he cannot take both; whether he should buy pleasure through extravagance, or hold on to his money through greed; whether he should go to the circus or the theater, if both happen to be open on the same day; or, as a third option, whether to break into someone's house, if he has the chance; or, fourth, whether to commit adultery, if he happens to have the means for that too, at the very same moment — all these possibilities meeting together at the same point in time, and all equally desired, though they cannot all be done at once; for they tear the mind apart among four, or even more, conflicting wills, given the vast range of things people desire, and yet they still do not claim that there are that many different substances at work. The same holds for good wills. For I ask them: is it good to take pleasure in reading the Apostle? Or good to take pleasure in a solemn Psalm? Or good to discuss the Gospel? To each of these they will answer, "It is good." What, then, if all of these give equal pleasure, and all at the same time? Do not different wills pull the mind apart, while it deliberates which one it should choose instead? And yet all of them are good, and they remain in conflict until one is chosen, toward which the entire will, previously split among many, can now be carried whole. In the same way, when eternity draws us upward with delight, and the pleasure of some temporal good holds us down below, it is the very same soul that does not will either one with an entire will, and so it is torn apart by painful conflict, because out of truth it puts one first, while out of habit it does not set the other aside.

So I was sick in soul, and in torment, blaming myself far more harshly than usual, twisting and turning in my chain until it should be utterly broken — the chain by which I was now only barely, but still, held fast. And you, Lord, pressed upon me in my innermost parts with a severe mercy, doubling the lashes of fear and shame, in case I should give way again, and, failing to snap that same slender remaining bond, it should grow strong again and bind me all the tighter. For I kept saying to myself, "Let it happen now, let it happen now." And as I said this, I very nearly acted on it. I very nearly did it, and did not do it — yet I did not slide back into my former state either, but stood my ground close by, and caught my breath. And I tried again, and came a little closer than before, and a little closer still, and very nearly touched it and took hold of it — and yet I did not reach it, and did not touch it, and did not take hold of it; hesitating to die to death and to live to life; and the worse habit I was used to had more power over me than the better one I was not used to; and the very moment in which I was to become someone other than I was — the closer it drew to me, the greater the horror it struck into me; yet it did not drive me back, or turn me away, but held me hanging in suspense.

The mere toys of toys, and emptiest of empty things, my old mistresses, still held onto me; they tugged at my garment of flesh, and whispered softly, "Are you casting us off? And from this moment will we never be with you again? And from this moment will this or that never again be permitted to you?" And what was it that they were suggesting, in what I called "this or that" — what were they suggesting, my God? Let your mercy turn it away from the soul of your servant. What filth they were suggesting! What shame! And by now I heard them far less than half as clearly, not openly showing themselves and arguing against me, but muttering, as it were, behind my back, and secretly tugging at me as I walked away, to make me look back at them. And yet they did hold me back, so that I hesitated to break free and shake myself loose from them, and leap over to where I was being called — while a violent habit kept saying to me, "Do you really think you can live without them?"

But by now it was speaking very faintly. For on the side toward which I had turned my face, and toward which I trembled to go, there appeared to me the chaste dignity of Continence, calm and serene, yet not slack or careless, cheerful, honestly urging me to come and not hesitate, stretching out her hands to receive and embrace me, hands full of great crowds of good examples: there were so many young men and young women there, a crowd of youth of every age, grave widows and elderly virgins, and Continence herself present in all of them, not barren, but the fruitful mother of children born of joy, by you, Lord, her husband. And she smiled at me with a persuasive mockery, as if to say, "Can you not do what these young men and these young women can do? Or can they do it by themselves, and not rather in the Lord their God? The Lord their God gave me to them. Why do you stand on your own strength, and so fail to stand at all? Throw yourself on him, don't be afraid — he will not pull away and let you fall; throw yourself on him without fear, he will catch you, and heal you." And I blushed deeply, because I could still hear the muttering of those trifles, and I hung there undecided. And she seemed to say again, "Stop your ears against those unclean parts of you that belong to the earth, so that they may be put to death. They tell you of pleasures, but not as the law of the Lord your God does." This struggle in my heart was nothing but myself against myself. But Alypius, sitting close beside me, waited in silence to see how this unfamiliar turmoil of mine would end.

But when a deep reflection had, from the hidden depths of my soul, dragged together and heaped up the whole of my misery before the sight of my heart, a huge storm rose up in me, bringing with it a huge downpour of tears. And so that I could let it all out, with its natural sounds, I got up and left Alypius: solitude struck me as better suited to the business of weeping, so I went far enough away that even his presence could not weigh on me. That was how it was with me then, and he sensed something of it; for I think I had said something in which the tones of my voice already sounded choked with weeping, and that was when I had stood up. He stayed where we had been sitting, utterly astonished. I threw myself down, somehow, under a certain fig tree, and let my tears pour out freely, and the flood from my eyes burst out as an offering acceptable to you. And, not in these exact words, but to this effect, I said much to you: and you, Lord, how long? How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? Do not remember our past wrongs — for I felt that I was still held fast by them. I sent up these sorrowful words: How long, how long, "tomorrow, and tomorrow"? Why not now? Why is there not this very hour an end to my uncleanness?

So I was speaking, and weeping in the most bitter contrition of my heart, when, suddenly, I heard from a nearby house a voice, a boy's or a girl's, I don't know which, chanting, and repeating over and over, "Take up and read; take up and read." At once my expression changed, and I began to think hard whether children ever sang words like that in any kind of game; and I could not remember ever having heard anything like it. So I checked the flood of my tears and stood up, taking it as nothing other than a command from God to open the book and read the first passage I came upon. For I had heard about Antony, that coming in during the reading of the Gospel, he took what was read as a message spoken directly to him: "Go, sell everything you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me"; and by that sign he was immediately converted to you. So I hurried back to the place where Alypius was sitting, for that was where I had left the volume of the Apostle when I got up. I snatched it up, opened it, and read in silence the passage my eyes fell on first: "Not in reveling and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and promiscuity, not in quarreling and jealousy, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to satisfy its desires." I did not want to read any further, nor did I need to, for instantly, at the end of that sentence, it was as though a light of certainty had been poured into my heart, and every shadow of doubt melted away.

Then, marking the place with my finger, or something else, I closed the book, and with a calm face I told Alypius what had happened. And what had happened within him, which I did not know, he showed me in this way. He asked to see what I had read; I showed him; and he looked further than the point I had read to, and I had not known what came after. What followed was this: "Welcome the one who is weak in faith" — which he applied to himself, and told me so. And by this word he was strengthened, and, by a good resolve and purpose entirely in keeping with his character, in which he had always differed from me very much for the better, he joined me without any anxious hesitation. From there we went in to my mother; we told her; she rejoiced. We told her, step by step, how it had happened; she leaped for joy in triumph, and blessed you, who are able to do far more than we ask or imagine; for she saw that you had given her, concerning me, more than she used to beg for with her pitiful and deeply sorrowful groaning. For you converted me to yourself, so that I no longer sought a wife or any hope in this world, standing firm on that same rule of faith on which you had shown me to her, so many years before, in a vision. And you turned her mourning into joy far more abundant than she had desired, and in a much dearer and purer way than she had ever looked for, through grandchildren of my body.
